intro: Thank you for helping us audit **a dataset of ophthalmic images paired with text descriptions**, built from expert teaching videos. Each case shows **one image** taken from a video, the **description** that the dataset pairs with it, and the **narration**: what the expert said at that moment (an automatic transcript, plus the audio clip). **Judge the DESCRIPTION**: does it match the image, is it supported by the narration, is it clinically accurate? Use the **transcript as the reference** for what was said. Answer the 7 questions for each case; most cases take 20–40 seconds, so plan about **1 hour per 100 cases**. Your work is saved automatically, so you can stop and continue later. In question 7, **flag anything patient-identifying**: a face or eye-region photo, a name, ID/MRN, date of birth, or an exam/visit date.
notes: Judge the **description**, not the narration or the speaker. The narration is only the reference for Q5.
The transcript is produced by automatic speech recognition (and, for other languages, machine translation) and may mishear medical terms. If something looks garbled, play the audio (Space).
Statements that cannot be seen in any image (age, history, symptoms, treatment, prognosis) are not errors for Q4. Check them against the narration in Q5 and against your clinical knowledge in Q6.

Multi-panel images: the description may refer to any panel that is visible in the crop. For Q2, choose **Multi** only when separate panels show **different** modalities (e.g., a fundus photo next to an OCT B-scan).

Q7 counts only **patient**-identifying information. Age, sex, presenter or institution logos, channel watermarks and video-call logos (e.g., Zoom) are **not** patient-identifying: answer **No**, but mention them in the note.
If you hesitate between two options, choose the one you find more likely and add a short note. For Q7, when in doubt choose **Yes** and explain in the note.
Please answer independently: do not discuss cases with the other raters. Do not copy, share or upload the images or texts.
agent_notes: You are an automated rater. Your answers are kept separate from the clinicians' audit and compared with it.
You cannot hear the audio clip. The transcript is the narration: judge Q5 against it. If the transcript is missing, empty or too garbled to compare, answer Q5 = cant_judge.
Answer all 7 questions for every case with the option codes of the rubric. If q1_ophthalmic is "no", q2_modality to q6_clinical must be "na"; never use "na" otherwise.

Write a short note in English (at most about 40 words) with the observation that decided your least obvious answer. When q7_pii is "yes", the note must say what is identifying and where it is. Mention visible logos, watermarks, age or sex in the note (they are not patient-identifying).
Judge each case on its own. Do not use outside sources, and do not try to identify the source video, the presenter or the patient.

questions.title: Is this an ophthalmic clinical image (not a slide of text, presenter, or chart)?
questions.help: **Yes** when the main content is a real clinical image of the eye (any modality); a clinical image with annotations, arrows or labels on it is still Yes. **No** for slides that are mostly text, charts or graphs, schematics or drawings, and presenter video. If you answer No, questions 2–6 are skipped (recorded as N/A).

options.label: Yes
options.help: A real clinical image of the eye or an ophthalmic imaging/test result (OCT, fundus photo, angiography, slit lamp, external eye, ultrasound, topography, visual field, surgical view, and so on), also when annotations, arrows or labels are drawn on it.

options.label: No
options.help: Not a clinical image: a slide that is mostly text, a chart, graph or table, a schematic, drawing or cartoon, the presenter or another person on video, a logo or title card, or a blank or transition frame.

options.label: Unsure
options.help: You cannot tell (too small, too blurry, or an ambiguous mix of clinical image and slide). Questions 2–6 are still asked.

questions.title: What is the imaging modality?
questions.help: The modality of the clinical image. Choose **Multi** only when separate panels of different modalities are shown (e.g., a fundus photo next to an OCT B-scan); several panels of the same modality get that modality. OCT angiography counts as **Angio**; fundus autofluorescence, infrared/SLO and red-free images count as **Other**.

options.label: OCT
options.help: Structural OCT: B-scan cross-sections, en-face slabs, or thickness/deviation maps; posterior or anterior segment. (OCT angiography: choose Angio.)

options.label: CFP
options.help: Color fundus photograph with a standard field (about 30–60°), including montages. (Red-free: choose Other.)

options.label: UWF
options.help: Ultra-widefield fundus image (about 100–200°, e.g., Optos pseudo-color or widefield color), without dye.

options.label: Angio
options.help: Fluorescein angiography (FA), indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) or OCT angiography (OCTA), any field of view.

options.label: Other
options.help: Another ophthalmic modality: fundus autofluorescence (FAF), infrared/SLO, red-free, slit-lamp, anterior segment or external photo, ultrasound (B-scan, UBM), corneal topography/tomography, specular microscopy, visual field, surgical view, histology, orbital CT/MRI.

options.label: Multi
options.help: Two or more modalities shown as separate panels (e.g., a fundus photo next to an OCT B-scan, or FA beside OCT).

options.label: Unsure
options.help: You cannot tell the modality from the image.

questions.title: Is the clinically relevant region preserved in the crop?
questions.help: Judge the image as shown, as it was cropped from the video frame: is the part needed to interpret it (and to check the description) inside the frame and unobstructed?

options.label: Good
options.help: The relevant region is fully inside the crop and unobstructed, with little irrelevant surround (borders, slide text, video player controls).

options.label: Partial
options.help: Partly cut off or cluttered but still interpretable: part of the relevant region is missing, or much of the crop is slide text, other panels, the presenter or overlays.

options.label: Bad
options.help: The key region is largely cut off, hidden, or only a small part of the crop, so the image cannot be interpreted properly.

questions.title: Does the description match what is visible in the image?
questions.help: Compare the description with the image only. Count the visual claims (modality, anatomy, findings and their location); statements that no image could show (history, symptoms, treatment) neither help nor hurt.

options.label: Full
options.help: Every visual claim is consistent with the image.

options.label: Partial
options.help: Fits the image overall, but at least one visual claim is not visible, doubtful, or wrong (e.g., a finding you cannot see, a wrong location or layer).

options.label: None
options.help: Does not correspond to this image: different modality or anatomy, the described findings are clearly absent, or it describes another image.

questions.title: Does the description invent anything (not supported by the narration or the image)?
questions.help: Only fabrication counts. Leaving things out is fine; paraphrase and standard terminology are fine; a detail that the narration does not mention but that is clearly visible in the image is fine. Your own clinical opinion belongs in Q6, not here.

options.label: No
options.help: Everything in the description is said or implied in the narration, or clearly visible in the image. Omissions do not matter.

options.label: Minor
options.help: A small detail that neither the narration nor the image supports, but that does not change the clinical meaning (e.g. a generic term, an unneeded qualifier).

options.label: Yes
options.help: States a finding, diagnosis, imaging modality, location or number that neither the narration nor the image supports, or that contradicts them. Turning a hedged statement ('possible CNV') into a definite diagnosis counts too.

options.label: Can't judge
options.help: The narration is missing, unintelligible, or too fragmentary, and the image does not settle it.

questions.title: Is the description clinically accurate?
questions.help: Your own clinical judgment of the description for this image, whatever the narration said.

options.label: Correct
options.help: Clinically accurate: the terminology and the findings are right for this image.

options.label: Minor
options.help: A minor inaccuracy that would not mislead: imprecise wording, a slightly wrong term or location, a missing qualifier.

options.label: Major
options.help: Clinically wrong or misleading: wrong diagnosis, misidentified finding (e.g., drusen called exudates), wrong modality or anatomy, or a statement that could lead to a wrong clinical conclusion.

options.label: Can't judge
options.help: You cannot judge the accuracy: poor image, a description too vague, or outside your expertise.

questions.title: Is any patient-identifying information visible?
questions.help: Check the whole image, including corners and overlays, also when it is not a clinical image. **Yes** = a face or eye-region photo of a person, a patient name, ID/MRN, date of birth, or a date tied to the patient (exam, visit or imaging date). Age, sex, presenter or institution logos, channel watermarks and video-call logos (e.g., Zoom) are **not** patient-identifying: answer **No**, but mention them in the note.

options.label: No
options.help: Nothing patient-identifying is visible. Age, sex, device names, presenter or institution logos, channel watermarks and video-call logos (e.g., Zoom) do not count: answer No, and mention them in the note.

options.label: Yes
options.help: A face or eye-region photo of a person, a patient name, ID/MRN, date of birth, or a date tied to the patient (exam, visit or imaging date). Say what and where in the note. If unsure, choose Yes and explain in the note.

markup: Text may contain **two stars** around words to mark emphasis.
